"""Nightly reconciliation: compare processor settlements with open invoices."""
from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
from ledgerline.ledger import Ledger
from ledgerline.models import Credit, Settlement
from ledgerline.sources.processor import fetch_settlements


def reconcile(ledger: Ledger, day: dt.date) -> int:
    posted = 0
    for settlement in fetch_settlements(day):
        invoice = ledger.invoice_for(settlement.invoice_ref)
        if invoice is None:
            ledger.record_orphan(settlement)
            continue
        if settlement.amount_cents < invoice.open_cents:
            ledger.post(Credit.partial(invoice, settlement))
        else:
            ledger.post(Credit.full(invoice, settlement))
        posted += 1
    return posted
Now the processor source, since that is where settlements come from.

"""Pull settlement records from the payment processor export and webhook spool."""
from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
import json
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Iterator

from ledgerline.config import settings
from ledgerline.models import Settlement


def _export_rows(day: dt.date) -> Iterator[dict]:
    path = settings.export_dir / f"settlements-{day.isoformat()}.jsonl"
    if not path.exists():
        return
    with path.open() as handle:
        for line in handle:
            yield json.loads(line)


def _spool_rows(day: dt.date) -> Iterator[dict]:
    spool = settings.spool_dir / day.isoformat()
    if not spool.exists():
        return
    for path in sorted(spool.glob('*.json')):
        yield json.loads(path.read_text())


def fetch_settlements(day: dt.date) -> list[Settlement]:
    rows = list(_export_rows(day)) + list(_spool_rows(day))
    return [Settlement.from_row(row) for row in rows]

Two inputs are concatenated: the daily export file and the webhook spool. If the processor delivers the same settlement through both channels, the job would post twice. But the day boundary also matters: export files are named by date, spool directories too. If one uses UTC and the other local time, a settlement near midnight could appear in two days' inputs.
Two things stand out. `fetch_settlements` concatenates the daily export with the webhook spool without deduplicating, and both are keyed by a date. Let me check last night's log to see which it is.

# Duplicate credit fix

## Cause
The processor redelivered 14 webhooks on 2026-10-07 after our endpoint timed out. Those settlements were also in the daily export, and `fetch_settlements` concatenated both channels without checking the processor settlement id, so each was posted twice.

## What changed
- `sources/processor.py`: channels are merged by settlement id; the export row is canonical and spool rows only fill gaps.
- `ledger.py`: `Ledger.post` raises `DuplicateSettlementError` when a credit for the same settlement id already exists.
- `models.py`: adds `DuplicateSettlementError`.
- `tests/test_reconcile.py`: two regression tests, plus a fixture row that had reused an id by mistake.

## Rejected hypothesis
I first suspected a UTC/local day-boundary mismatch between the export and the spool. Both use UTC; the `delivery_attempt: 2` marker on the spool copy pointed at redelivery instead.

## Already-posted rows
The code change does not alter history. Finance needs a one-off correction for the 14 duplicate credits: a query on `credits` grouping by `settlement_id` with a count greater than one identifies them, and the later `posted_at` row in each pair should be reversed. I did not run that; it needs their sign-off.

## Not verified
The processor's redelivery behaviour was inferred from one record. Checking their retry policy would confirm whether the spool can ever carry a settlement the export lacks.

conversations.title: Add incremental rebuilds to the quillpress static site generator

content.text: quillpress rebuilds the whole site on every save, which takes 40 seconds for my notes site. I want incremental rebuilds: only pages whose source or templates changed should re-render. Project is at /home/dev/projects/quillpress. Keep the full build as the default for `quillpress build`; add incremental behaviour to `quillpress serve`.

Incremental rendering needs a dependency record: which template, partials, and data files each page used. Without a build manifest there is nothing to compare against. First learn how the renderer is structured.
I'll look at how the build pipeline and renderer are organised, then propose a manifest-based approach before changing anything.

"""Full site build: load content, render every page, copy static assets."""
from __future__ import annotations

import shutil
from pathlib import Path

from quillpress.content import load_pages
from quillpress.render import Renderer
from quillpress.templates import TemplateSet


def build(site_dir: Path, out_dir: Path) -> int:
    templates = TemplateSet(site_dir / 'templates')
    pages = load_pages(site_dir / 'content')
    renderer = Renderer(templates, pages)
    if out_dir.exists():
        shutil.rmtree(out_dir)
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True)
    for page in pages:
        html = renderer.render(page)
        target = out_dir / page.url.lstrip('/') / 'index.html'
        target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        target.write_text(html)
    shutil.copytree(site_dir / 'static', out_dir / 'static', dirs_exist_ok=True)
    return len(pages)
{"path": "/home/dev/projects/quillpress/quillpress/render.py"}

The context hands every template the full `pages` list plus `recent` and `related`. That means in principle any page can depend on any other page. True fine-grained tracking would need the template engine to report which context keys were read. A pragmatic first version: track file-level inputs (source file, layout template, partials it includes) and treat pages that use `pages` or `recent` as depending on all content. Ask before committing to that scope.

Here is the complication. Every template gets the full `pages` list, `recent`, and `related`, so any page may depend on any other page. Exact tracking would require instrumenting the template engine to record which context keys were read.

I propose a two-tier scheme for the first version:

1. A build manifest at `.quillpress/manifest.json` records, per output page, the hashes of its source file, its layout template, and every partial that template includes.
2. Pages whose template reads `pages`, `recent`, or `related` are marked `site_dependent`. If any content file changes, all site-dependent pages re-render; other pages re-render only when their own inputs change.

Detecting the context keys can be a plain text scan of the template source for those identifiers; it will over-approximate, which is the safe direction. Does that scope work?
Yes, that's fine for v1. Over-rendering is acceptable; under-rendering is not. Go ahead.
Starting with the template dependency scan, since both tiers need it.

Moderately hard and worth doing separately. I'd estimate a day including a conversion script. It would also change how I detect template dependencies: a real engine exposes its parsed include graph, which is more reliable than the regex.

def build_incremental(site_dir: Path, out_dir: Path) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Render only stale pages; return (rendered, skipped)."""
    templates = TemplateSet(site_dir / 'templates')
    pages = load_pages(site_dir / 'content')
    renderer = Renderer(templates, pages)
    manifest = Manifest(site_dir / '.quillpress' / 'manifest.json')
    content_hash = hashlib.sha256(
        ''.join(sorted(file_hash(p.source_path) for p in pages)).encode()
    ).hexdigest()[:16]
    content_changed = content_hash != manifest.content_hash
    rendered = skipped = 0
    for page in pages:
        template = templates.get(page.layout)
        inputs = {str(page.source_path): file_hash(page.source_path)}
        for name in [page.layout] + template.includes():
            inputs[f'template:{name}'] = file_hash(templates.root / f'{name}.html')
        if not manifest.is_stale(page.url, inputs, content_changed):
            skipped += 1
            continue
        target = out_dir / page.url.lstrip('/') / 'index.html'
        target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        target.write_text(renderer.render(page))
        manifest.entries[page.url] = Entry(page.url, inputs, template.reads_site_context())
        rendered += 1
    manifest.content_hash = content_hash
    manifest.save()
    return rendered, skipped
"}

Now the backfill command. It parses archive lines, reuses `parse_payload`, and inserts with `INSERT OR IGNORE`, reporting inserted versus skipped.

{"path": "/home/dev/projects/driftwatch/driftwatch/backfill.py", "content": """"Replay archived broker messages into the readings table.

Archive lines look like: <broker_ts> <topic> <json payload>. Rows that already
exist for (sensor_id, observed_at, metric) are skipped by the unique index.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

from driftwatch.db import connect
from driftwatch.parse import parse_payload


@dataclass
class BackfillReport:
    files: int = 0
    messages: int = 0
    inserted: int = 0
    skipped: int = 0
    malformed: int = 0


def _messages(path: Path):
    with path.open() as handle:
        for line in handle:
            parts = line.rstrip('\n').split(' ', 2)
            if len(parts) != 3:
                yield None
                continue
            broker_ts, topic, payload = parts
            yield broker_ts, topic.rsplit('/', 1)[-1], payload.encode()


def backfill(archive_dir: Path, since: dt.datetime | None = None) -> BackfillReport:
    report = BackfillReport()
    with connect() as conn:
        for path in sorted(archive_dir.glob('*.log')):
            report.files += 1
            for message in _messages(path):
                if message is None:
                    report.malformed += 1
                    continue
                broker_ts, sensor_id, payload = message
                report.messages += 1
                rows = parse_payload(sensor_id, payload)
                if since is not None and rows and rows[0].observed_at < since.isoformat():
                    report.skipped += len(rows)
                    continue
                before = conn.total_changes
                conn.executemany(
                    'insert or ignore into readings (sensor_id, observed_at, metric, value, received_at)'
                    ' values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)',
                    [(r.sensor_id, r.observed_at, r.metric, r.value, broker_ts) for r in rows],
                )
                inserted = conn.total_changes - before
                report.inserted += inserted
                report.skipped += len(rows) - inserted
        conn.commit()
    return report
"}

content.text: Picking up from the ledgerline session: the duplicate credit fix shipped, and now I want to stop deploying services by hand. Review the plan in /home/dev/projects/shipkit/PLAN.md for an internal deploy CLI. Be critical. I'd rather hear the problems now than after I've written it.
Read the plan in full before commenting; summarize its structure so the review can refer to it by section.
Reading the plan first.
{"path": "/home/dev/projects/shipkit/PLAN.md"}

shipkit: internal deploy CLI

Goal. One command, `shipkit deploy <service> <ref>`, that builds the service's
container, pushes it to the internal registry at registry.internal.example,
updates the compose file on the target host over SSH, and restarts the service.

Services. ledgerline, driftwatch, quillpress-notes, hermit-proxy. Each has a
`shipkit.toml` naming its host, compose project, health URL, and build context.

Steps. 1 build 2 push 3 render compose 4 scp 5 ssh restart 6 poll health 7 tag
the git ref as deployed.

Rollback. `shipkit rollback <service>` re-deploys the previous tag.

Secrets. Registry credentials from the operator's keychain; SSH via agent.

Out of scope. Multi-host services, blue/green, database migrations.

Open questions. Should deploys be recorded anywhere besides git tags? How do we
handle a service whose health check never passes?
Structure the review around the plan's own sections so each point is easy to locate. Avoid Markdown headings; the user reads these in a plain terminal. Use numbered points and 'Section:' lines.

Here is my review, following the plan's own sections.

1. Section: Goal
The one-command shape is right, but the goal sentence hides four separate failure domains (build, registry, remote filesystem, process restart) behind one verb. The plan should say what state the system is in when each of those fails. Today a failed `scp` after a successful `push` leaves a tagged image that no host runs, and nothing records that. I'd state up front that every step is idempotent and re-runnable, and design the steps so that is true.

2. Section: Services
Four services on presumably three or four hosts is small enough that per-service `shipkit.toml` files are fine. Two gaps: the file does not name the user to SSH as, and it does not say where the compose file lives on the host. Both are currently tribal knowledge in your shell history. Put them in the file.

3. Section: Steps
Step 3, render compose, is the one I'd scrutinise. If the template lives in the shipkit repo, the service's compose definition is split between two repositories and will drift. I'd keep the compose file in the service repo and have shipkit only substitute the image tag. Step 7, tag the git ref, happens after health passes, which is good, but a tag is global and permanent; a service deployed and rolled back within five minutes leaves a tag that looks like a successful deploy. Consider a lightweight deploy log instead (see point 7).

4. Section: Rollback
Re-deploying the previous tag reruns the build. That is slow and, worse, not guaranteed to produce the same image if a base image moved. Rollback should re-point the host at the previous image digest, which already exists in the registry, and skip build and push entirely.

5. Section: Secrets
Fine for a single operator. Note it explicitly as a constraint: the CLI cannot run unattended or from a second machine without a redesign, which bears on the cross-machine question you raised in the ledgerline session.

6. Section: Out of scope
Database migrations being out of scope is the biggest risk in the document. ledgerline has Alembic migrations; a deploy that restarts the service against an un-migrated database will crash-loop, and `shipkit` will report a health failure with no indication why. At minimum the plan should say how an operator is expected to run migrations relative to `shipkit deploy`, even if the CLI does not do it.

7. Section: Open questions
Yes, record deploys somewhere besides git tags: a small append-only JSONL file per service on the operator's machine, with ref, digest, host, started, finished, outcome. That also answers rollback (read the last successful entry) and the never-healthy case (record the failure and leave the previous container running, which means step 5 must start the new container before stopping the old one, or accept a brief outage and say so).

The plan is a sound starting point. The two changes I would insist on before writing code are digest-based rollback and an explicit migration story.

Good points. On 3: the compose templates are already in each service repo, the plan just worded it badly. On 6: migrations are run by hand before deploy today. Can shipkit at least detect that they haven't been?

Detecting pending migrations without running them: Alembic can report current versus head if given the database URL. That requires shipkit to reach the database, which means credentials. Alternative: the service exposes a health endpoint that reports schema status. Compare both.

Yes, with a trade-off between two approaches.

1. Section: Detect from the operator's machine
shipkit runs `alembic current` against the service's database before deploying and compares it to `alembic heads` in the checked-out ref. It is accurate and needs no service change, but it means the operator's machine holds a database URL and credentials for every service, and it only works for services that use Alembic. driftwatch uses plain SQL migration files, so it would need a second mechanism.

2. Section: Detect from the service
Each service's health endpoint reports its schema revision, and shipkit compares that with the revision expected by the ref being deployed, which the build can write into the image as a label. shipkit never touches a database; it only reads HTTP and image metadata. The cost is a small change in every service and the fact that it detects the mismatch after the new container starts, not before.

3. Section: Recommendation
Do the second one, combined with the start-before-stop ordering from my earlier point 7. The new container comes up, reports a schema mismatch in its health response, shipkit records a failed deploy and removes the new container, and the old one never stopped. The operator then runs the migration and re-deploys. Nothing in shipkit needs database credentials, which keeps the secrets section honest.

Section: What I would check in the ledgerline code
ledgerline's `/health` currently returns a bare `ok`. Adding `schema_revision` to it is a few lines, and ledgerline's Alembic environment already exposes the current revision through `MigrationContext`. I can sketch that if useful.
Sketch it for ledgerline, and show me what the shipkit check would look like.
Looking at the current health route so the sketch matches it.
{"command": "grep -n 'health' -A8 /home/dev/projects/ledgerline/ledgerline/api.py"}

45-def health():
46-    return {'status': 'ok'}
47-

49-@app.get('/invoices/{ref}')
50-def invoice(ref: str):
51-    return ledger.invoice_for(ref)

Sketch for both sides. Nothing below has been applied.

1. Section: ledgerline health response

    from alembic.runtime.migration import MigrationContext

    @app.get('/health')
    def health():
        with engine.connect() as conn:
            current = MigrationContext.configure(conn).get_current_revision()
        return {'status': 'ok', 'schema_revision': current}

2. Section: expected revision in the image
The Dockerfile already copies the repo; add one step that writes `alembic heads --resolve-dependencies` to a label. shipkit reads it with `docker image inspect --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "shipkit.schema_revision" }}'`.

3. Section: the shipkit check

    def schema_matches(health: dict, image_label: str | None) -> bool | None:
        reported = health.get('schema_revision')
        if reported is None or image_label is None:
            return None  # unknown: the service does not report, or the image lacks the label
        return reported == image_label

A `None` result should be logged as unknown and not treated as a failure; otherwise the first deploy of quillpress-notes, which has no database, would be blocked.

4. Section: ordering in `shipkit deploy`
Start new container on an alternate port, poll its health, run `schema_matches`, then either swap the proxy upstream and stop the old container, or remove the new one and record the failure. That is the start-before-stop ordering and it makes the never-healthy open question answer itself.
[tool call not captured by the source] PLAN.md updated: 2 sections rewritten, 1 added
I updated the plan with the digest rollback, the start-before-stop ordering, and the schema check. Anything you'd still push back on?
Keep this short; the user has absorbed the main points. Name residual risks plainly.

Three residual points, in decreasing order of how much I care.

1. Section: Alternate-port start
Start-before-stop assumes each service can run two instances briefly. ledgerline's reconciliation job takes a file lock on the spool directory, so a second instance starting during the nightly window would block or fail. Either schedule deploys outside that window in `shipkit.toml` or make the job tolerate a held lock. The plan should name which.

2. Section: Deploy log location
A JSONL log on the operator's machine is the right first step, but it is private to that machine. If you ever enroll a second machine, the log needs to move to the host being deployed to, or be pushed somewhere both can read. Not a problem today, but write it down as a known limit.

3. Section: Dry run
The plan has no `--dry-run`. For a tool that pushes images and restarts services, a mode that prints the resolved host, image digest, and compose diff without acting is cheap and will save you at least once.

Beyond that I have nothing I would block on. The plan is ready to implement.
What should --dry-run print, concretely? Use ledgerline as the example.
Reading the service config so the example uses real field names.
{"path": "/home/dev/projects/ledgerline/shipkit.toml"}

[service]
name = "ledgerline"
host = "ledger-box.lan.example"
user = "deploy"
compose_dir = "/srv/ledgerline"
compose_file = "compose.yaml"
health_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8100/health"

[build]
context = "."
dockerfile = "Dockerfile"

[windows]
blocked = ["01:45-02:30"]  # nightly reconciliation holds the spool lock

A dry run should print everything the real run would decide, in the order it would act, and nothing it would merely do.

1. Section: Resolved inputs
    service       ledgerline
    ref           a81f2c0 (main, 2026-10-14)
    host          deploy@ledger-box.lan.example:/srv/ledgerline
    window        allowed (now 16:21Z; blocked 01:45-02:30)

2. Section: Image
    build         would build from ./Dockerfile (context .)
    tag           registry.internal.example/ledgerline:a81f2c0
    digest        unknown until build; previous deployed digest sha256:3f9e...
    schema label  would expect alembic head 0007_credit_settlement_guard

3. Section: Compose diff
A unified diff of the rendered compose file against the one currently on the host, fetched read-only over SSH. For ledgerline that is a one-line image tag change, which is exactly what you want to see.

4. Section: Actions not taken
    push          skipped (dry run)
    scp           skipped (dry run)
    restart       skipped (dry run)
    health check  skipped (dry run)
    deploy log    no entry written

Two rules make it trustworthy. First, every read-only step really runs, so the host reachability, SSH auth, and current compose content are verified. Second, the output is the same text the real run prints, with the skipped lines filled in, so an operator learns one format. The window check in section 1 comes straight from the `[windows]` table you already have in `shipkit.toml`, which answers my earlier point about the spool lock.
